title: March 2026 Trade Review
description: Trade Recap - Here's What I've Been Buying and Selling
body_html:

The S&P is down 1.34% YTD, practically unchanged. After a 25.95% SPX return in 2023, 25.00% in 2024, and 17.86% in 2025, this should feel like nothing, but Fintwit seems to be singing a different tune. To their credit, things really do feel different.

Underneath the headline -1.34% figure, whipsaw and dispersion are at the highest levels since 2008.

The whipsaw isn’t even limited to sector-vs-sector, sub-sector volatility is also raging. As an example, the broader Real Estate Index is up 6.29% yet Office REITs have plunged more than 21%. Financials are down 7%, yet Regional Banks were up nearly 14% at one point and are still clinging on to tiny YTD gains. To top it all off, traditionally sneered-at capital-intensive sectors such as Commodities, Chemicals, and Oil & Gas are leading the way with 30%+ returns.

Fund Flows are notably different. For the first time in years, QQQ inflows are flat while investors clamor into RSP (the Invesco Equal Weighted S&P ETF) and the Korea craze continues as investors remain undeterred by the largest drop since 2008.

While it is easy to blame these moves on the Iran War or Tariff Policy, most of them have been bubbling up since the beginning of the year and I think the widespread rotation and dispersion was bound to happen anyways.

The rose-colored glasses we had on for the last three years are coming off, and the AI bull case that powered a two-year “everyone is a winner” rally in everything aside from a few phone-support stocks (Five9, Concentrix, etc) seems to be increasingly two-sided. These days, it seems one name’s AI Bull Case is another’s Bear Case.

Pieces such as Citrini's Global Intelligence Crisis have gone viral, and I think these thought exercises are valuable: the World is changing at a light-speed pace, and it’s worth questioning assumptions and asking “what if’s” to see if your thesis is still compelling.

Just this weekend, Bloomberg reported Stripe and Circle are racing to build their own payments systems for autonomous agents. I’m sure you’re skeptical, so am I. But also consider in 2022 AI was a gimmick that made pixelated videos of Will Smith eating spaghetti, and now in just a few sentences, you can draw up a lifelike-video with near Hollywood quality. Tools like Claude and Shortcut can save minutes, even hours in Excel. Claude Code and Codex aren’t perfect, but they can turn one man into a one man army.

Just imagine where things are in a few years.

If Visa, Mastercard, and Amex are unwilling to let their payments systems be used for autonomous transactions (due to concerns over chargebacks or fraud), someone will create a system that will. In 5, maybe 10 years, you might forget to buy Valentine’s day chocolates and flowers, and perhaps you can load a Claude or OpenAI “Wallet” with 100 USDC or PYUSD (PayPal’s stablecoin) and simply tell it what you want it and where it should be delivered. Is this a certainty? Of course not. But there is a slim chance it happens, and the disruption risk it represents is easy to understand when many names trade at historical valuation highs and shareholders emphatically claim “it won’t happen”.

As an aside, even after Amex’s 20% December - March drawdown, Amex still trades at just a 2% discount to the 5-Year historical valuation average.

I’m the last guy to call a top, and in fact, I’m not going to. But from a stock-picker’s perspective, I think 2026 is shaping up to be fundamentally different: the playbook of piling into large-cap “quality” regardless of the multiple is no longer working, and I think this is when active management and conservative position sizing (keeping names below 10%) begins to shine, especially when it comes to steering clear of value traps such as troubled Software Oriented BDCs, no matter how cheap they appear.

Since I’ve started this blog, I’ve covered about 50 different trades, most of which are still open, across Financials (Banking and Insurance), AI Infrastructure and Memory, and Global Equities. Over the past two weeks, I’ve been making many adjustments to my portfolio: I’ve entirely closed a few winners, been stopped out on a loser, raised cash to 20%, and added 2 new names where I think the risk-to-reward is compelling despite the current turmoil.

To be entirely transparent with you, my Portfolio is heavily skewed towards Small Cap Value and International Equities. The S&P Regional Bank Index has a market cap of less than $600 Billion (a tiny fraction of the S&P 500’s $59.94 Trillion), and countries such as Sweden, Japan, Australia, Georgia, Canada, and Kazakhstan make up less than 10% of the World’s Market Cap, but a much larger portion of my Portfolio.

As a result, in this Trade Review I’m going to cover the trades I am in, what I’ve been trimming, what I’ve been adding to, and my conviction on each trade, but ultimately the weights are up to you to determine. I want this blog to be a place to see ideas and setups you might not usually see, when I write up Small Cap setups such as International General Insurance, CBL Properties, Chain Bridge Bancorp, and Georgia Capital, it’s to get these names on your radar. It’s entirely up to you to conduct your own due-diligence, determine if you find the thesis attractive, whether these trades are suitable for your portfolio, and of course what the appropriate weight might be.

The Trade Review is organized into:

  1. Trade List and Performance Review

  2. Trade History - Removals and Hedging

  3. Trade History - Additions and New Positions

  4. General Commentary and Conclusion

Trade List and Performance Review

(If the image is blurry, downloading to Desktop makes it clear)

Despite last week’s turbulence, it’s been a decent start to the year. I’ve combed through all of the articles, the chat, and my posts on Twitter to compile and benchmark the performance of each trade, including the ones I closed this week.

For the purposes of calculating performance, I computed the Total Return between the date the trade was first posted to the present, March 6th, 2026 (or trade closure if applicable). While my cost basis on Comfort Systems and Western Digital is below what is reflected in the sheet, it wouldn’t be right to use that basis as the entry point - each total return is the price appreciation + dividends after the trade was posted on here or on Twitter. For trades like OP Bancorp and Heritage Insurance that were opened and closed at previous profits, I am entirely excluding previous gains and only using the most recent re-entry as the starting point to compute returns.

The 48 trades are ordered by conviction, and then by initial entry date. A green trade denotes an existing position I have been adding to or a brand new position. A red trade denotes a position I closed, or in the case of UVE (Universal Insurance Holdings), a new short position. A reddish pink trade denotes a position I am trimming (in the case of KRNY Kearny) or hedging by purchasing puts and selling calls against (in the case of FIX, WDC, and POWL, and to a lesser extent IESC). This week I raised cash by another 10% to 20%.

An equal-weight average of the trades is +9.15% YTD (led by Samsung, Powell, 9478 JP, Oppenheimer, Comfort Systems) and median performance is +3.84%. A few high conviction Long Trades are lagging, notably OSB Group, Customer’s Bancorp, Ambea Group, and OP Bancorp, but given the broader Financials benchmark is down 7% and Regional Banks have plummeted 12% in a matter of days, I think relatively minimal moves of 5-10% YTD on these trades is acceptable, I’m not surprised to see a bit of volatility given the recent run.

The AI Infrastructure trades, Powell Industries, Comfort Systems, and IES Holdings, as well as the Memory and Storage trades, Western Digital, Kioxia, Samsung, and Hynix, have delivered the bulk of the YTD returns. Frankly, I think they are headed for a rough couple of weeks, which is why I posted the hedge ideas in the chat. Comfort Systems has had ferociously strong earnings reports and continues to report record backlog levels, but also seems overextended on a short-term basis and is a victim of its own success: as people pile in and become accustomed to 10% Revenue beats and a 30% EPS beats, the bar moves higher and higher each quarter. Eventually, someone will get concerned. My conviction on Comfort Systems and Powell Industries has thus dropped to “Low”, if you are sitting on a position with a smaller capital gain (and a lower resulting tax bill if you sell), and are unable to hedge with options, I wouldn’t really fault you for trimming here as an alternative to hedging.

In addition to getting brutally stopped out on the Power Solutions International position on Monday, I’ve been harvesting profits in Financials winners, Stonex Group, Conduit Insurance Holdings, Commercial BancGroup, taking a loss on American Integrity Insurance, as winding down a few Preferred Stocks since I think the risk-to-reward is no longer as favorable as it once was.

Trade History - Removals and Hedges

1. Removed: Stonex Group (Profit: +185%)

Stonex (SNEX US) was one of my original pitches, and over the last two years has transformed from a deep-value Financial intermediary setup to a growth name the market has clearly discovered. Despite the recent market volatility, which should drive strong earnings in its Brokerage and Physical Commodities business, after consistent re-rating from just 8x earnings to nearly 14x I think the value setup for Stonex simply doesn’t exist. Whenever market volatility occurs, the conversation consistently shifts from “volatility is good” to “too much volatility could cause a customer to implode”, which obviously weighed on both Stonex and Marex on Friday. I certainly don’t think Stonex is a short here, but simply put I think it makes sense to harvest profit and keep that powder dry for more compelling opportunities.

I’ve also paused my purchases of Marex. Marex is no stranger to volatility, Metals market making is one of their largest segments, and given they handled massive gold and silver volatility and Q4 and Q1, I think they have solid risk management in place. Nonetheless, trying to catch a falling knife is difficult, and just as MRX, SNEX, and IBKR performed last March and April over concerns the bond basis trade was imploding and customers would be insolvent, I think similar concerns will arise as long as the crude volatility continues. I wish I could bang the table as a bull all the time, but just as how I soured on FIX and POWL despite owning them, I think the near-term volatility will heavily impact perception of brokers and in particular, commodity futures oriented brokers such as Marex and Stonex, so in MRX’s case I am preserving dry powder to add once things calm down.

2. Removed: Conduit Insurance Holdings (Profit: +12.8%)

Conduit Insurance Holdings (CRE LN) was a value setup from the February 3rd piece. The impetus for the trade was the deep discount to Tangible Book (25% at the time), and the fact closely comparable peers had already reported strong results. With the earnings pop out of the way and an unfavorable environment for reinsurance in 2026, I think it is time to take profits on Conduit. The company can probably continue to repurchase large amounts of stock and engineer decent returns for the next few months, but ultimately Conduit is perceived as an “underperformer” in the eyes of insurance analysts, and upside is likely limited to 0.9x Tangible Book unless they are bought, simply put there isn’t much upside left on the trade.

3. Removed: Commercial BancGroup (Profit: +6.5%)

Commercial BancGroup (CBK US) was a special situations Bank IPO setup from last October. For a brief moment, CBK traded sharply below the IPO price of $24. At the current price, it trades at roughly 1.25x Tangible Book and 8.8x 2026 Earnings, cheap relative to the market, but essentially in-line with closely comparable peers. Frankly, I think the setup for Regional Banks may be difficult in the upcoming months and I think CBK will trade relatively in line with the index, I’d rather convert the position to cash, lock in a profit, and leave dry powder in the event bargains emerge over the next couple of months.

4. Removed: Centene Corp (Profit: +12.8%)

I added Centene Corp on October 3 as a short-term setup in the hopes the government would announce a massive extension in ACA subsidies. Since then, the House of Representatives has passed a 3-year extension, but the bill has been stuck in the Senate and is unlikely to be passed. When market volatility erupts, I like to step away from lower conviction positions, Centene is certainly not a high conviction setup for me and I’m pleasantly surprised to see it trading so well while peers like UNH continue to trend down. Was happy to lock in a 12% profit and convert the position into cash.

5. Removed: American Integrity (Loss: -1%)

Despite American Integrity’s strong results, the lack of a share repurchase program left me disappointed. Among peers (HRTG, SLDE, HCI, UVE, ACIC), American Integrity trades at the cheapest Price to Tangible Book Ratio, and is also sitting on significant excess capital. The company’s decision to pay out a large special dividend, and stated goal of increasing the float

“We wanted to get our stock in the hands of new public shareholders that understand our business that are excited the way we are about our future growth prospects, and provide the float and the daily volumes necessary to create liquidity and make our stock attractive to investors.

So because that was a decision point, we didn’t want to take float out of the market today.”

appeared to be a stark contrast to peers such as HCI, who indicated a much more bullish capital allocation.

Ultimately, I think the problem with hyper-regional insurers such as Kingstone and American Integrity is they are highly vulnerable to declining insurance rates given they have very little geographical diversification. Kingstone is in the process of a small expansion to California and American Integrity has a growing presence in South Carolina, but insurance investors are forward-looking and concerns about declining rates in Florida and Long Island leave little room for error. My favorite “regional” insurance idea is Heritage Insurance (HRTG US), which is about to report earnings tomorrow and highly likely to “beat” the $1.74 consensus estimate since they have already pre-reported EPS is expected to be above $2.00 a share.

What I like about Heritage is Heritage is the competition, unlike Kingstone and American Integrity who are playing defense, Heritage is playing offense. They aren’t necessarily expanding into new geographies, rather, they are ramping up underwriting in areas they previously had sizeable market share. One of Kingstone’s primary competitors in the Long Island area is Narragansett Bay Insurance who is owned by, you guessed it, Heritage.

At roughly 7x forward earnings and 1.15x Tangible Book American Integrity is by no means expensive - I wish I could consistently bang the table on all cheap insurance names, but here I don’t think there is much upside ahead. The stock is trading right just below the initial entry of $19.60, I am happy to take a small loss and retain the capital for more attractive opportunities.

6. Removed: Power Solutions International (Loss: -7%)

I was blindsided by Power Solutions International (PSIX US) this past week. For high volatility names like PSIX (or even WDC for that matter), I always collar my position prior to earnings by selling a deep out of the money call and purchasing close to the money puts. PSIX typically reports in the middle to end of March, and after the run up to $100 and the subsequent fall to $82, I was getting ready to put on a spread to protect the $15 a share in unrealized gains.

The early report, lack of substantial commentary, and relatively unimpressive results caught everyone off guard. I’m a firm believer in limiting losses to 10-15% below your initial entry, and getting even more stringent with names after a massive run up. Of course, on names that have doubled or even tripled since entry such as Comfort Systems or Western Digital leniency and flexibility is reasonable since you don’t want to blow out your tax bill and sell a winner on a small retracement , but for PSIX that pain point was a few dollars below my entry of $66, and by the time I was able to close out my position on Monday it had already dropped to $62. Absent a change in management style where commentary and visibility is given outside of private investor meetings, I will not be revisiting this name. This week’s move was painful - while a 7% loss is manageable, it was beyond painful to watch a 60% gain turn red in a matter of days.

7. Trimming: Kearny Bancorp (Gain: +15%)

Kearny Bancorp was featured in the "Shifting Into Rates Down" piece from last August, and has performed well since. The stock still trades at just 0.74x Tangible Book Value of $9.93, but my senses tell me banking bargains are ahead, and I have been lightening the position up in the $7.50 - $7.75 range. At $7, I am happy to sit on my position at 9x earnings, 0.7x Tangible Book, and collect a 6% dividend yield, but in the $7.50 - $7.75 range I have orders to lighten up my position and make room for new opportunities.

8. Hedging: Western Digital, Comfort Systems, Powell Industries, IES Holdings

Hedging on Western Digital (WDC US), Comfort Systems (FIX US), Powell Industries (POWL US), and IES Holdings (IESC US) is highly dependent on your position size and cost basis. Of the four, the only one trading at a reasonable valuation (and in fact, a sub-market P/E) is IES Holdings.

What I mean by “dependent on position size and cost basis” is you don’t necessarily want to sell Comfort Systems or Powell Industries if you are sitting on a 100%+ gain (triggering a sizeable tax bill), but you also might be bearish short-term on the name. If so, many of these names still have significant call-skew, and you can hedge your position by selling March calls 8-9% above the current price, and purchasing March puts 7-8% below the current price at a small credit (or by simply purchasing puts outright). This avoids realized gains and substantially locks in most of your profits should another rough week occur. If your gain in Comfort Systems, Powell, or Western Digital is not too significant and you don’t mind taxes, or you own fewer than 100 shares and are uncomfortable with options, I really wouldn’t blame you for closing out - I think the near-term risk-to-reward is balanced at best, and there will probably be a decent opportunity to re-enter in the near future once things calm down.

The only name within the group I’m not too concerned about after the recent fall is IES Holdings. I think their differentiated approach of providing a wide variety of electrical services while slowly buying out the supply chain and parts manufacturers is a winning strategy, and that as time goes on the market will begin to warm to IES given that it trades at just 24x forward earnings, roughly in-line with the S&P.

9. Trimming GNL-B and MBINL

GNL Preferred Series B and MBIN Series L have performed well since we added them, and both still offer respectable 7% dividend yields. Nonetheless, with a 2% profit in GNL-B and a 9% profit in MBINL, I think it makes sense to convert the position to cash as 7% isn’t such a compelling yield - I’d rather have the proceeds as dry powder and use them to purchase equities I find compelling.

Trade History - New Positions and Additions to Existing Positions

1. Adding to OSB Group (OSB LN)

OSB is a specialist mortgage lender with a high concentration in buy-to-rent and commercial financing. OSB’s specialist underwriting talent and consistently strong capital return initiatives continue to impress - the company continues to remain overcapitalized and has plenty of capacity for further shareholder returns, as illustrated by the fresh $100 Million Share Repurchase program and the 6% dividend.

At a 2% discount to book, 7x forward earnings, and a share repurchase program amounting to 2% of shares outstanding, I think OSB is one of the only “cheap” British banks remaining, and will eventually be a takeover candidate given its underwriting talent could be highly accretive to larger banks that trade at 9-10x earnings and sizeable premiums to Tangible Book.

I’ve been slowly adding shares around 570, and plan to get more aggressive should the shares trade down into the 550’s.

2. Adding to SE Holdings and Incubations (9478 JP)

SE Holdings and Incubations is my highest conviction Japanese pick, it’s a sleepy publisher with a massive Securities Portfolio hidden beneath the surface. The stock trades at 470 Yen, a sizeable discount to my estimated Q1 Tangible Book Value of 720 Yen, likely because SE’s unrealized equity gains never flow through to earnings since it doesn’t touch its portfolio. The company has regularly exhibited excellent capital allocation, using profits from the publishing business and interest and dividends from its investments to repurchase nearly 10% of shares outstanding each year since 2021 (more details on the 9478 pitch are here).

I like to anchor my entries around the company’s recent share repurchases - the February 2026 Share Repurchase Report indicated repurchases at an average price of 466 Yen, so I have set up orders in the 450 - 460 Yen range. The company has authorization to repurchase an additional 188 Million Yen (400,000 shares) this month, and I think share repurchases at just 0.65x estimated Tangible Book are highly accretive and demonstrate the company is acutely aware the stock is undervalued. Despite recent volatility, I’m still bullish on Japanese equities, and 9478 remains my preferred way to get exposure at a deep-discount to Net Asset Value. I don’t expect the discount to close anytime soon, given SE’s small market cap and thin liquidity it’s unlikely it ever trades at a premium, but as long as the excellent capital allocation continues, I am happy to be a shareholder and I think the company will make steady progress on narrowing the discount.

3. Adding to Modern Dental Group (3600 HK)

I have been steadily adding to Modern Dental Group ahead of 2025 H2 earnings. Modern Dental Group (3600 HK) is a global dental prosthetics manufacturer headquartered in Hong Kong, but its largest markets are Europe (48%) and North America (22%), where it operates 80 dental labs under local banners. This innovative, local approach has allowed it to steadily swallow up regional competitors without being slapped with a “foreign” or made-in-China stigma since products are manufactured locally.

Earnings have consistently grown at an 8% pace since 2021, and Hillhouse Investment Management, a healthcare-oriented Private Equity Firm, recently acquired 17% of the company from one of the founding families at $5.80, a sizeable premium to where it was trading. I believe Modern Dental Group is largely insulated from tariffs, wars, AI, and should continue to grow as its highly aligned management (50% is owned by the founding family along with 17% by Hillhouse) continues to execute. At 10.5x forward earnings, it trades with the usual “HK Discount”, but Modern Dental Group’s history of dividends, share repurchases, and success, as well as the fact a well-respected Private Equity firm conducted enough due diligence to purchase a sizeable stake, leads me to believe that discount is wrongly applied - if the name traded in Europe or America it would almost certainly trade at a higher valuation. It’s a boring position and is unlikely to surprise to the upside, but over time I expect it continue to chug along, and with concerns mounting over AI, energy prices, and geopolitical strife, I think Modern Dental Group represents a rare opportunity to buy an insulated business at a relatively inexpensive multiple.

4. Adding to Kaspi (KSPI US)

Kaspi (KSPI) has spent the better part of the last year in the doghouse as investors punished the management team for pouring cash into the Hepsiburada acquisition in Turkey instead of returning it to shareholders. That narrative is finally shifting as Kaspi just announced an 850 KZT dividend per ADS, roughly $1.71 per quarter, which equates to a 9% yield at current prices.

Kaspi is a “superapp” in Kazakhstan, their proprietary payments, e-commerce marketplace, travel, lending, and grocery divisions dominate the country. Practically every Kazakh adult uses Kaspi. While the government has taken action to “open up” Kaspi’s QR payments division (to allow clients with bank accounts at other institutions to also receive payments), Kaspi’s position in e-commerce is unchallengeable, and remains highly linked to a growing Kazakh economy.

Kazakhstan itself is primed for an excellent 2026, with prices for its primary exports (Crude, Gold, Uranium, Copper, and Chromium) soaring. The prospect of a strong currency not only benefits Kaspi (since it is priced in USD), it also opens the door to Kazakh rate-cuts, which will heavily benefit Kaspi’s banking segment and lower the “implied cost of capital” analysts use to justify why Kaspi should trade at a low multiple.

With a massive 9% dividend yield now in place, I believe the bottom for Kaspi is finally in. Kaspi is a growth name trading at a deep-value multiple, and I think the recent share buyback program paired with the long-awaited resumption of the dividend is enough to change the narrative. Concerns about growth in the fintech segment often don’t account for the “upside”: banking is a capital intensive business and slower than expected growth simply frees up more cash to be returned in the form of repurchases and dividends. Based on the current multiple and implied 9% yield, I think a more reasonable valuation for Kaspi would be $90 a share, implying a 7.5% dividend yield and 7.5x 2026 earnings. Until a more premium valuation is reached, I am happy to slowly add to my position at 6x forward earnings and collect a sizeable dividend.

5. Adding to Itafos (IFOS CN)

Contributor: Karst Research

Itafos is a small Fertilizer Producer with operations in the United States (Idaho) and Brazil. Itafos is attractive on a standalone basis, trades at roughly 4x EV / EBITDA, and has built a substantial cash balance (98 Million CAD) that exceeds its debt (82 Million), making it one of the only fertilizer names with a clean balance sheet. The company is arguably already in a “critical industry” given the importance of fertilizer, and recent disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz are poised to spike phosphate-based fertilizer prices higher given Saudi Arabia and Qatar account for nearly 40% of US Phosphate imports.

Itafos is able to source sulfuric acid needs locally, and rising phosphate-fertilizer prices represent a windfall to a dname that trades at just 4x forward earnings. With a substantially clean balance sheet, a heavily aligned Private Equity Owner (Castlelake owns 66% of shares) and the company finally turning the capital-return spigot via two special dividends in 2025, I think Itafos provides an under-the-radar opportunity that is standalone attractive, and is probably the only name in my portfolio that stands to gain from turmoil in the Middle East.

6. New Position: Entravision (EVC US)

After earnings on Friday, I bought a speculative starter position in Entravision.

Entravision is a special situation: its legacy media TV and Radio stations are structurally challenged and in a slow decline, while its rapidly growing Adtech segment (Smadex) continues to post record numbers.

Advertising Technology and Services revenue was up 123% YOY, and Operating Profit surged from $2 Million to $12 Million while overall results painted a much less rosy picture with Net Income of -$23 Million, primarily driven by a $26 Million Impairment Charge. Ultimately, I think Entravision is bound to pursue a strategic transaction, the sale or spin of its Smadex segment.

13% of the company is held by Gate City Capital Management, and 15% is held by Alexandra Seros, the widow of the previous Chairman Walter Ulloa. I think an enterprising banker is bound to stumble upon Smadex, realize there is significant value to be unlocked from separating the divisions, and make a compelling pitch to effectuate a spinoff. To be upfront, Entravision is a buy now investigate later position for me. I was stunned by how impressive their Q4 and 2025 Smadex results were, but I also didn’t buy in large size and am waiting to see how others receive the results, given SOTP stories rely heavily on perception until an actual spinoff occurs, I think this is a name to monitor and see if the Smadex results attract analyst and Institutional attention.

7. New Short Position: Universal Insurance (UVE US)

UVE is a FL Insurer with a specialty in Apartments. Despite strong results driven by almost zero catastrophe losses in 2025, I think UVE is over-earning and significantly above its historical valuation at an 80% premium to Tangible Book Value. While 8x earnings may not seem like an expensive valuation, insurance rates are clearly going down, and I believe UVE’s current valuation will not be sustained as competition soars and a significant decline in 2027 insurance rates becomes more obvious.

The short position in UVE is small for me, and is intended to cancel out my long position in HRTG given they both cover similar geography (although HRTG has exposure to California, New York, and the broader South). I think a much more reasonable valuation for UVE would be 1.6x Tangible Book, which implies $32 a share.

General Commentary and Conclusion

I’m not a macro guy and I generally don’t bet against the market - when volatility increases I step away from positions I have less conviction in to raise cash. This past week, in addition to raising a bit of cash and collaring WDC, IESC, FIX, and POWL, I put 1% into SPX June 6600 Puts. I’m happy to lose 1% if a fast resolution to the Iran situation is reached, and otherwise it serves as a small hedge given most of these trades are up YTD and I’m still 80% net.

During turbulent times, I think it’s ok to say “I don’t know”, and incorporate that into your positioning. Assuming the market opens down 2.5% tomorrow, the YTD S&P return is -4%, yet the mood feels much more negative since many are emphatically claiming a bottom and buying the dip with leverage. Just as how it would’ve been excruciatingly painful to try to time a “top” for names like Hynix and Samsung, I think it is also excruciatingly difficult to time a bottom and go “all in”.

Tomorrow will be a rough day. My approach remains the same as it has been: stay disciplined, hold your best ideas at a comfortable weight (< 10%), and don’t be forced into decisions you’ll regret in either direction. The investors who get hurt most in volatile markets are those who either panic-sell the lows, or those who leverage up after proclaiming a “bottom” just a week into a drawdown.

Moving forward, I will be making these recaps monthly. I know many of you don’t trade actively or have time to check the chat - while I will continue to post any time sensitive updates in the chat, these monthly recaps will track performance, cover new positions, and adjustments to existing trades.
